name: sample-rust-error-handling
description: Rust Error Handling Pattern for NDP: Use thiserror for library errors and anyhow for application errors. Steps: 1) Define custom error enum with #[derive(thiserror::Error, Debug)], 2) Use #[error("message")] for display, 3) Implement From<T> for error conversion, 4) Return Result<T, Error> from all fallible functions. Example: pub enum SourceError { #[error("Connection failed: {0}")] Connection(String), #[error("Parse error")] Parse(#[from] serde_json::Error) }

Design Principles: 1) Domain-agnostic core (core/ crate), 2) Domain-specific adapters (domains/, apps/), 3) Configuration-driven behavior (YAML → etcd), 4) Trait-based dependency inversion. name: arch-data-lake-layers

SILVER (TimescaleDB): Analytics, dashboards - Schema-on-write (typed columns). GOLD (Features/ML): Predictions, aggregations - Derived from Silver. name: arch-dual-trait-source

RawSource trait: fetch_raw()/fetch_raw_batch() → RawDataPoint for raw JSON (Bronze layer). CRITICAL: Only RawSource::fetch_raw_batch() is called in production. Production Flow: main.rs → IngestionCoordinator → SourceManager → source.fetch_raw_batch() → RawDataPoint → ParquetStore. Parser configs remain in stream config for future Silver ETL. Problem Solved: Double polling caused memory accumulation and Pi lockups. Status: Implemented.

name: arch-http-polling

Error Classification: Transient (5xx, network) → Exponential backoff, Rate Limited (429) → Parse Retry-After, respect quota, Permanent (401, 403, 404) → Log error, skip endpoint. Health Check Pattern: Staleness detection - Alert if no data for 2× poll_interval. Status: Implemented.

name: arch-mcp-response-format

Double serialization required by MCP spec. Alternatives rejected: Plain text (not parseable), multiple content items (splits info), no success flag (less explicit). name: grafana-timescaledb-migration
description: Grafana Dashboard Migration - DuckDB to TimescaleDB. Key SQL patterns: 1) Time filter: DuckDB uses timestamp >= ${__from}::BIGINT * 1000, TimescaleDB uses $__timeFilter(time). 2) Time bucketing: Both use time_bucket() but TimescaleDB prefers string intervals ('10 minutes' vs INTERVAL). 3) Data access: DuckDB reads Parquet with read_parquet(), TimescaleDB queries tables directly. 4) Current value queries: DuckDB needs subquery with LIMIT, TimescaleDB is simple ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT 1. Performance: Use continuous aggregates (hourly/daily) for time ranges >24h. Connection pooling: maxOpenConns=5, maxIdleConns=2 for Pi constraints. Refresh rates: Overview=1m, Detail=5m, Historical=15m. See research/agenticdataplatform/silver/04-dashboard-integration.md for complete guide.

name: grafana-alerting-timescaledb

Alert timing: evaluation interval 1m, for duration 5-15m depending on metric volatility. Query pattern: SELECT time, metric as value FROM silver.table WHERE time > NOW() - INTERVAL '5 minutes' ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT 1. Use Grafana expressions for reduce and threshold conditions. Labels: severity (warning/critical), stream (stream_id). Provisioning via YAML in config/grafana/provisioning/alerting/. Convert source units to SI standards at ETL time: Temperature (Kelvin/Fahrenheit -> Celsius), Pressure (Pa -> hPa), Wind speed (km/h, mph -> m/s), Visibility (miles -> meters). Store unit metadata in column comments or data dictionary. Pattern: source_value * conversion_factor + offset. Examples: OWM temp: K-273.15, NWS wind: km_h/3.6, Fahrenheit: (F-32)*5/9. name: ml-dq-monitoring
description: ML-Specific Data Quality Monitoring Pattern. Beyond basic range_check/not_null, ML pipelines need: DISTRIBUTION DRIFT: Monitor KL divergence from reference window (30 days), alert when >0.1. NULL RATE: Track % nulls per column per 24h window, alert if exceeds threshold. OUTLIER DETECTION: z-score (threshold 4.0) and IQR (3x multiplier) methods, flag don't remove. TEMPORAL CONSISTENCY: Max gap detection, rate-of-change plausibility. TRAINING DQ REPORT: Before training - feature completeness, correlation matrix, label distribution, temporal coverage, outlier summary. Config example: ml_dq_rules: [{type: distribution_drift, column: X, reference_window: 30d, alert_threshold: 0.1}]. Tags: ml, dq, data-quality, drift-detection, outliers, mlops.

name: dq-framework-design
description: Config-Driven DQ Framework Pattern (DP-006). 11 DQ rule types: range_check, null_check, enum_check, pattern_check (value-level); freshness_check, monotonic_check, rate_of_change (temporal); cross_field_check, conditional_check (cross-field); completeness_check, cardinality_check (batch-level). Actions: flag (default, preserve data), reject (set NULL), clamp (adjust to bounds), drop (exclude row). dq_flags column: TEXT[] with format '{rule_type}:{field}:{reason}[:{value}]'. Transparency tables: silver.dq_transparency (row-level audit), silver.dq_batch_summary (batch metrics), silver.dq_metrics_hourly (continuous aggregate). Key principle: Flag over reject - preserve data, enable investigation. Domain-specific thresholds in config YAML. name: silver-layer-schema-evolution
description: Adding new columns to Silver layer tables via config-driven migration
code:
## Schema Evolution for Silver Layer

### Overview
The Silver ETL supports adding new columns to existing TimescaleDB tables through config-driven migrations. This is useful when you need to add new fields to an existing stream without losing historical data.

### Workflow: Adding a New Field

1. **Update stream config** (config/base/streams/{stream}/config.yaml):
   ```yaml
   silver_etl:
     field_mappings:
       # Existing fields...
       - source_field: 'raw_payload.humidity'  # NEW
         target_field: 'humidity'
         target_type: 'DOUBLE PRECISION'
   ```

2. **Sync config to etcd**:
   ```bash
   ./deploy.sh sync
   ```

3. **Run migrate** (handles ALTER TABLE automatically):
   ```bash
   ./deploy.sh silver-migrate
   # Or dry-run first:
   ./deploy.sh silver-migrate --dry-run
   ```

4. **ETL will populate new field for future records**:
   ```bash
   ./deploy.sh silver-etl
   ```

### How It Works

The migrate command:
1. Connects to TimescaleDB
2. Queries existing columns via `information_schema.columns`
3. Compares with config's `field_mappings`
4. Generates `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` for new columns
5. Executes DDL

### Key Files
- `apps/silver-etl/src/main.rs`: `migrate_schema()` and `query_existing_columns()`
- `apps/silver-etl/src/schema_gen.rs`: `generate_add_columns()`

### Important Notes
- New columns will be NULL for existing rows
- To backfill historical data, use the (future) `reload` command
- Column types must match neural_core::config types (double_precision, text, etc.)
- All migrations use IF NOT EXISTS for idempotency

name: duckdb-timestamptz-arithmetic
description: DuckDB TIMESTAMPTZ Arithmetic Pattern - CRITICAL for Silver ETL. DuckDB does NOT support direct TIMESTAMPTZ arithmetic. All timestamp interval/subtraction operations must cast to TIMESTAMP first. WRONG: observation_time < ingestion_time - INTERVAL '3 hours'. CORRECT: observation_time::TIMESTAMP < (ingestion_time::TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '3 hours'). WRONG: observation_time - LAG(observation_time). CORRECT: observation_time::TIMESTAMP - (LAG(observation_time) OVER (...))::TIMESTAMP. WRONG: SELECT MAX(timestamptz_col) returning native type. CORRECT: SELECT MAX(col)::VARCHAR for string handling. Applies to: dq.rs (freshness_check, rate_of_change), sql_gen.rs (incremental WHERE), etl.rs (watermark queries). TimescaleDB handles TIMESTAMPTZ natively - this is DuckDB ETL layer only. Tags: duckdb, timestamptz, timestamp, interval, silver-etl, sql-generation, dp-006, dp-007.

name: proc-multi-stream-sync
description: Multi-Stream Data Dictionary Sync Procedure - dp-009. When multiple Bronze streams feed one Silver table, use UPSERT (not TRUNCATE) sync strategy: (1) Two-pass collection: First pass builds associative array mapping Silver tables to list of source streams; (2) source_streams[] aggregation: Array of all streams feeding this table; (3) Lineage preservation: Keep all mappings from all contributing streams; (4) UPSERT with ON CONFLICT: Update existing rows, insert new ones atomically. Example: outdoor-weather + nws-observations both feed silver.weather_observations. Each contributes different fields but share table. Sync must preserve lineage from both while avoiding duplicates. Query: WHERE daemon_cycle_id = X shows correlated failures. Orphan handling: 1) Startup cleanup marks stale running > 15min as failed, 2) pg_cron hourly cleanup for edge cases. Status values: running, success, failed (partial is computed at cycle level for MCP). Error handling: Persistence failure logged but does NOT fail ETL. name: architecture:event-bus-broadcast
description: ADR-012-001: Use tokio::broadcast for in-process multi-consumer event broadcasting. Key decisions: (1) tokio::broadcast channel instead of external broker - no network overhead, simple deployment, Pi-appropriate, (2) Arc<RawDataPoint> for zero-copy event sharing, (3) capacity: 10,000 events with lag_warning_threshold: 1,000, (4) Events dropped when buffer full (oldest first), (5) Not suitable for distributed deployment without redesign. Rationale: < 1ms broadcast latency, 1000+ events/sec capacity, easy to test, future-proof (can add external broker later). Consequences: subscribers must catch up from Bronze if they lag/crash since message history not preserved. Related files: core/src/event_bus/mod.rs

name: architecture:subscriber-isolation
description: ADR-012-002: Each subscriber runs in its own tokio task, spawned by SubscriberCoordinator. Key decisions: (1) Independent tokio tasks per subscriber (not sequential processing or separate processes), (2) JoinHandle for health monitoring, (3) SubscriberCoordinator manages lifecycle. Rationale: Task panic doesn't crash the application, each subscriber has own receive loop and buffering, independent backpressure handling, easy to add/remove subscribers dynamically. Consequences: All share same process memory limits, CPU-intensive subscriber could starve others (mitigated by async nature). Use this pattern when you need multiple consumers that should be isolated from each other's failures. Related files: core/src/subscribers/coordinator.rs

name: architecture:streaming-catchup

Key principle: Bronze is source of truth - already durable via WAL, no duplicate storage needed for Silver. Rationale: Zero data loss on restart, handles lag gracefully, simple implementation. Consequences: Startup time proportional to catch-up window, requires Bronze to be available. Use UPSERT for idempotency - duplicates from catch-up + streaming overlap are handled gracefully. Rationale: Separation of concerns, reusability (pattern works for thresholds, anomaly detection, etc.), easy to add new processor types. name: data:upsert-idempotency
description: UPSERT pattern for idempotent Silver writes in DP-012: Use ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE to handle duplicates safely. Why needed: (1) Catch-up on startup reads from Bronze which may overlap with already-written streaming data, (2) Retries after transient failures may re-send same records. Implementation: INSERT INTO table (...) VALUES (...) ON CONFLICT (primary_key) DO UPDATE SET column = EXCLUDED.column. Primary key typically includes stream_id + observation_time. This pattern ensures data is never lost and never duplicated regardless of restart timing or retry behavior. Related: architecture:streaming-catchup

name: operations:graceful-degradation
description: Graceful degradation priority order for DP-012 components: (1) Bronze write - MUST succeed (data durability), retry with backoff, eventually log critical error, (2) Silver write - SHOULD succeed, retry + backoff, will catch up on restart from Bronze, (3) Threshold alerts - Nice to have, skip if issues, log warning and continue, (4) Event notifications - Optional, fire-and-forget QoS 0, ignore failures. Error recovery matrix: EventBus full = oldest events dropped, Subscriber lagged = log warning continue, Bronze write fail = retry 3x, Silver DB down = retry + backoff + catch up on restart, Transform error = skip row continue, DQ rule fail = set dq_flags continue, MQTT down = ignore, Processor error = skip row continue.

name: dimension-table-sql-patterns
description: Dimension Table SQL Patterns for dp-013. (1) DDL: CREATE TABLE with PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL for required fields, audit columns (loaded_at, source_file). (2) Type mapping: text->TEXT, int->INTEGER, float->DOUBLE PRECISION, bool->BOOLEAN, timestamp->TIMESTAMPTZ, json->JSONB. (3) Load strategies: truncate_and_load (DELETE + INSERT in transaction) for full refresh, upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET) for incremental/merge. (4) Gold view pattern: LEFT JOIN dimension to hypertable using ndp_id, preserves records without context. (5) Migration: Add columns with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, remove columns requires dependency check first, type changes need migration script with data conversion. Key tables: silver.entity_context (ndp_id PK, category, friendly_name, location_path, correlates_with, orientation). See product/features/dp-013/architecture/SQL_PATTERNS.md for full documentation. Tags: dp-013, dimension, silver, sql, ddl, upsert, gold-view.

name: csv-dq-patterns
description: CSV Data Quality Patterns (dp-013). VALIDATION LAYERS: Layer 0 (Pre-Load) - file exists, readable, required columns present, config valid - all Fatal. Layer 1 (Parse-Time) - type conversion, timestamp parse, required fields - Streams: configurable skip/abort, Dimensions: always abort. Layer 2 (Post-Load) - PK uniqueness, row count, referential integrity - for dimensions only. ERROR BEHAVIOR: Dimensions always abort on error (must be complete). Streams default to skip (on_error: skip|abort configurable). ERROR CLASSIFICATION: Fatal errors - file not found, malformed CSV, missing columns, PK violation. Configurable errors - type conversion, timestamp parse. Warnings - empty file. TRANSPARENCY TABLES: silver.dimension_load_history (dimension_id, loaded_at, rows_before/after, strategy, success, source_file, report_json), bronze.csv_ingest_history (stream_id, ingested_at, rows_written/skipped, on_error_policy, skipped_rows JSONB). LOG FORMAT: [ERROR] dp-013/csv: Row N: message. CLI OUTPUT: Summary with total/processed/skipped counts, error details with line numbers. DRY-RUN: Validate without side effects via --dry-run flag. See product/features/dp-013/refinement/DATA_QUALITY.md for full specification.

name: csv-source-rust-patterns
description: CSV Source and Dimension Table Rust Implementation Patterns (dp-013). Key patterns: (1) CsvSource implements RawSource trait, produces RawDataPoint with row data as JSON in raw_payload, timestamp parsed from configured field. (2) DimensionLoader trait with CsvDimensionLoader implementation for loading reference data directly to Silver. (3) CsvSourceConfig: path, timestamp_field, timestamp_format (iso8601/epoch_seconds/epoch_millis/custom), delimiter, on_error (skip/abort). (4) DimensionConfig: dimension_id, target (table, primary_key), source (csv path), schema (fields), load (truncate_and_load/upsert). (5) Error types: CsvError with Parse/MissingField/TypeConversion/FileError variants, DimensionError with SchemaValidation/LoadFailed/TableCreation. (6) Module structure: core/src/sources/csv.rs for CsvSource, core/src/dimensions/ for loader. (7) Dependencies: csv-async crate for streaming parsing. (8) Batch inserts use transactions, multi-value INSERT for efficiency. Location: product/features/dp-013/refinement/RUST_IMPLEMENTATION.md.
